steps.title: Light and bright
steps.body: Corvina, or Corvina Veronese, is the main grape of Valpolicella, near Verona. On its own, it gives light to medium-bodied wines with sour cherry, red berries, almond and herbs. Colour is moderate, tannins are low, acidity is fresh. It's a very different wine before and after drying.

steps.title: Built for drying
steps.body: Corvina has thick skins, loose bunches and good resistance to rot, which make it ideal for drying grapes after harvest. During drying, it develops a compound profile rich in aromatic precursors, and its skins help resist mould. That's why it's the backbone of Amarone and Recioto.
steps.highlight: Thick skins and loose bunches for drying

steps.prompt: Why is Corvina well suited to drying?
options: Thick skins and loose bunches that resist rot
steps.explanation: Loose bunches let air circulate, and thick skins resist mould during months of drying.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: A simple Valpolicella is pale to medium ruby, with bright cherry and a slightly bitter almond finish. Amarone is deep, with dried cherry, raisin, chocolate and spice, and high alcohol. That bitter cherry and almond note links them all.
steps.highlight: Cherry with a bitter almond finish

steps.prompt: Corvina naturally gives deep-coloured, very tannic wines.
steps.explanation: Not true. Fresh Corvina is moderately coloured with low tannin. Drying gives Amarone its concentration.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Corvina gives sour cherry, almond and fresh acidity
Thick skins and loose bunches make it ideal for drying
Valpolicella's styles all share its cherry and almond
